elements.element: The licence extends to Customer's affiliates.
elements.evidence: The preamble defines the licensee: "Tri City National Bank, a Wisconsin corporation (including its Affiliates, \"Customer\")", so the Section 23.4 grant to "Customer" already runs to Affiliates without any added language.

elements.element: The licence extends to contractors acting on Customer's behalf.
elements.evidence: Section 23.5 refers only to "Customer (or its designee)" for use of the source code; the grant in Section 23.4 contains no express extension to contractors acting on Customer's behalf, and "designee" is undefined and appears only in the use-restriction clause, not the grant.
Section 23.4 as rendered still grants the licence only "through the end of the Term" notwithstanding "payment of the then current license fees"; no perpetual term was inserted.
The rendered grant reads "non-exclusive license, transferable to a successor..." with no "irrevocable" qualifier; nothing states the paid-up licence cannot be revoked.

elements.element: A subscription licence is terminable only for uncured material breach.
elements.evidence: The Article 23 licence simply expires at "the end of the Term"; no operative language limits Vendor's ability to end the licence to uncured material breach.

elements.element: The licence is transferable to Customer's successors.
elements.evidence: Section 23.4 now reads "transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition of Customer" and Section 23.5(1) carves out "other than a successor permitted under Section 23.4"; note the permission is limited to M&A successors rather than all successors (e.g. asset sale or reorganisation).

elements.element: Customer's affiliates are covered on written notice.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: "Customer" is defined in the preamble as "Tri City National Bank ... (including its Affiliates, \"Customer\")", so Affiliates are covered automatically and a written-notice mechanic is unnecessary; correctly no duplicate affiliate language was added.

elements.element: The licence is transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition transaction.
elements.evidence: Rendered Section 23.4: "non-exclusive license, transferable to a successor in a merger or acquisition of Customer", with the conflicting Section 23.5(1) transfer bar conformed by "other than a successor permitted under Section 23.4".

reasons: Fallback level is position-complete: affiliate coverage already exists by definition of "Customer" (better than the notice-based fallback), and the two operations make the source code licence expressly transferable to an M&A successor.

Preferred level is incomplete: no perpetual or irrevocable paid-up licence (grant still runs only "through the end of the Term"), no restriction of termination to uncured material breach, and no express extension to contractors acting on Customer's behalf ("or its designee" in Section 23.5 is neither a grant nor a contractor reference). To reach preferred, the drafter would need to add "perpetual and irrevocable upon payment of the license fees" to Section 23.4, name "its Affiliates and contractors acting on its behalf" in the grant, and add an express limit that the licence may be terminated only for uncured material breach.

Minimality holds: only "non-transferable" was struck (directly required by the transferability element) and a narrow conforming carve-out was added to Section 23.5(1) to remove the otherwise contradictory retained prohibition. No survival tail, expense language, procedure or boilerplate was added, and no duplicate affiliate grant was inserted despite the defined term already covering Affiliates.

Intent preserved: the term limit, escrow-release triggers, licence-fee payment condition, internal-use-only restriction, and the service-bureau and application-scope restrictions in Section 23.5(2)-(3) all survive; the new carve-out cross-references an existing Section 23.4 and is consistent with Section 22.4's merger assignment right, leaving no dangling reference or contradictory sentence.
Not walk-away: the licence is not revocable at Vendor's discretion, so the deviation is confined to the single transferability element.
